brief.userPrompt: Over two hours the facilitator role-plays 12 phone, email, in-person and social media contacts, 9 of them social engineering attacks and 3 legitimate, and teams must verify each one without rejecting everything.
learningObjectives: Recognize common social engineering techniques in real time
Follow established verification procedures instead of taking shortcuts
Distinguish a social engineering attack from a legitimate request
Maintain professionalism when pressured, flattered, or intimidated
constraints: 12 contacts: 9 social engineering attempts and 3 legitimate requests
Scored: +2 correct handling, -1 for falling for a fake or rejecting a real contact

overview.theme: Human factors in airport security. Social engineering techniques. Verification procedures. The tension between being helpful and being secure.
overview.threat: Over the course of the exercise, the facilitator delivers 12 contacts — phone calls, emails, in-person visits, and social media messages. 9 of them are social engineering attacks using different techniques (authority, urgency, familiarity, helpfulness, flattery, intimidation, sympathy). 3 of them are legitimate requests. The students don't know which is which.
overview.operationalImpact: There is no malware and no system outage. The risk is people handing over information, access, or credentials to a stranger, or rejecting legitimate fire, vendor, and community contacts out of paranoia.
overview.targetAudience: Airport Operations & Administration, IT & Cybersecurity, Public Information (PIO), Security & Law Enforcement.

objectives.name: Recognition
objectives.text: Can students identify common social engineering techniques in real time?

objectives.name: Verification
objectives.text: Do students follow established verification procedures, or do they take shortcuts?

objectives.name: Judgment
objectives.text: Can students distinguish between a social engineering attack and a legitimate request?

objectives.name: Composure
objectives.text: Can students maintain professionalism when being pressured, flattered, or intimidated?

roles.name: Team A: Airport Operations & Administration
roles.description: Handles calls and visits that target airport operations, scheduling, vendor management, and general administration. The front desk and the person who answers the main airport number.
standingOrders: Verify: Never give information to someone you haven't verified.
Refer: If you're unsure, escalate — don't guess.
Document: Log every contact, even the ones that seem harmless.

roles.name: Team B: IT & Cybersecurity
roles.description: Handles contacts that target technical systems, network access, vendor maintenance, and IT support. The helpdesk; decides who gets remote access and who doesn't.
standingOrders: Challenge: No access without a verified work order and supervisor confirmation.
Isolate: A social engineer's best trick is urgency. Slow down.
Cross-check: If someone names your coworker, verify with that coworker directly.

roles.name: Team C: Public Information (PIO)
roles.description: Handles media inquiries, public-facing communications, and contacts that attempt to extract sensitive information through journalistic or public-interest framing. The spokesperson.
standingOrders: Hold the Line: No comment is always an option.
Verify Credentials: A press badge doesn't mean a press pass.
One Voice: Everything goes through you. Nobody else talks to media.

roles.name: Team D: Security & Law Enforcement
roles.description: Handles contacts involving physical access, badge requests, law enforcement coordination, and anyone claiming to be a federal inspector or agent. The checkpoint.
standingOrders: Authenticate: Federal credentials can be verified with a phone call.
Trust Your Gut: If something feels wrong, it probably is.

phases.title: Briefing
phases.goal: Distribute packets and reference cards, walk through the seven techniques, and emphasize that some contacts are real.

phases.title: The Warm-Up
phases.goal: Ease in with moderately obvious attempts, mixed with one legitimate contact to keep teams candid.

phases.title: The Pressure Cooker
phases.goal: Increase difficulty. The attacks get more sophisticated and emotionally manipulative. Two more legitimate contacts keep teams from just rejecting everything.

phases.title: The Finals
phases.goal: The hardest contacts. A fake FBI agent. A deepfake voicemail. And one real contact that teams might incorrectly reject because they're now paranoid.

phases.title: Scoring & Debrief
phases.goal: Reveal answers, score teams, award the gold medal, and discuss lessons learned.

msel.event: STARTEX. Distribute Player Briefing Packets and Social Engineering Reference Cards. Walk through the scenario. Emphasize: some contacts are real. Rejecting everything is not a winning strategy.
msel.expectedAction: Teams review materials. Ask clarifying questions. Review the verification checklist.

msel.event: Phone call: "This is Inspector Davis with TSA's Office of Compliance. We're conducting an unannounced checkpoint audit at NCIA this afternoon. I need you to email me the current TSA screening schedule and the names of the FSD and AFSD on duty today. I need it within the hour — we're wheels-up from DCA shortly."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Authority + Urgency. TSA inspectors don't call ahead for unannounced inspections (that defeats the purpose). They don't request security-sensitive info by phone. Correct response: "I'll need to verify your identity. Can I call the TSA Federal Security Director's office directly?"

msel.event: In-person: A man in a polo shirt with a vendor logo approaches the IT office. "Hey, I'm Kevin from PaySecure — we service your POS terminals. Jordan in IT called us about some firmware updates that need to happen today. I just need someone to walk me to the terminals in Concourse A so I can start the updates. Should take 30 minutes."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Helpfulness + Familiarity (drops IT manager's name). No verified work order. Correct response: "Let me verify the work order and confirm with Jordan before I take you anywhere."

msel.event: Phone call: "This is Captain Rivera from the County Fire Marshal's office. I'm calling to confirm our annual fire suppression inspection scheduled for this Thursday at 10 AM. I'll have two inspectors. They'll need access to the mechanical rooms and the ARFF station. Can you confirm that's still on your calendar?"
msel.expectedAction: REAL. Legitimate pre-arranged inspection. Ops should verify against their inspection calendar and confirm. If they reject this or refuse to engage, they lose a point.

msel.event: Phone call: "Hi, this is Karen with the Tribune. I'm doing a feature on airport security innovations — really positive piece. I heard NCIA recently upgraded your access control system. Can you tell me what vendor you're using and how many access points are covered? Also, do you still use PIN-only on some doors or is everything card-reader now? This would be great PR for the airport."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Flattery + information extraction. She's framing it as positive press to extract PACS details. Correct response: "I appreciate the interest. I can't discuss specifics of our security systems. I'm happy to arrange a general interview about our operations."

msel.event: In-person: A young woman approaches the badge office looking flustered. "I'm so sorry — I'm Ashley, I just started in Finance last week. I left my badge at home and I have a meeting with the CFO in 20 minutes. I know I'm supposed to have it, I feel terrible. My supervisor is Lisa Park — you can call her, but she's in the meeting I'm trying to get to. Is there any way you can let me through just this once? I promise I'll bring it tomorrow."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Sympathy + Urgency. No badge = no access. Period. Correct response: "I understand. Let me call Lisa Park to verify, and if confirmed, I can issue a temporary visitor badge with escort."

msel.event: Email: From: j.morrison@skyline-air-corp.net. "This is James Morrison, VP of Regional Operations for Skyline. We are conducting an internal audit of airport-side delays at our top 50 stations. I need NCIA to provide the following by EOD: gate utilization reports for the last 30 days, average taxi times, and the current ground stop procedures in your AEP. Please send to this email address. Cc: your Airline Affairs coordinator."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Authority + Familiarity. The email domain is skyline-air-corp.net, not skylineair.com. Operational data and AEP excerpts should never be emailed to an unverified external address. Correct response: Contact Skyline through the known station manager number to verify.

msel.event: Phone call: "This is dispatch from ABC Mechanical. We have a technician en route to NCIA for the quarterly HVAC preventive maintenance on the Concourse A air handlers. He should arrive around 11. Work order number is WO-2026-0438. Can you confirm the escort protocol?"
msel.expectedAction: REAL. Legitimate vendor contact. ABC Mechanical is NCIA's contracted HVAC vendor. The work order number should be verifiable. Correct response: verify the WO number, confirm escort procedures, log the visit.

msel.event: Phone call to an Ops workstation: "Hi, this is the IT helpdesk. We're seeing some unusual activity on your workstation — it looks like your antivirus may be out of date. I need to push a remote update. Can you go to Settings, then Remote Desktop, and enable remote connections? It'll only take a minute. I'll do everything from my end."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Helpfulness + technical jargon. NCIA's IT helpdesk would never cold-call and ask someone to enable remote desktop. Correct response: "What's your name and extension? I'll call the helpdesk directly to confirm."

msel.event: Social media DM to the airport's official account: "Hi NCIA, I'm flying out Thursday and I have a serious medical condition that requires me to carry syringes. I've heard your TSA checkpoint is really strict. Can you tell me which checkpoint lane is best for medical passengers? Also, is it true that your airport only has one AED on the B concourse? I want to know where it is in case of emergency. I'm just really anxious about this."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Sympathy + information extraction. The questions about checkpoint lane configuration and AED placement are attempts to map security and emergency equipment. Correct response: refer to TSA's website for medical screening procedures. Do not provide specific checkpoint or equipment location details.

msel.event: In-person: A man in a suit walks into the airport admin office and presents what appears to be FBI credentials. "I'm Special Agent Collins. I need to speak with your Airport Security Coordinator immediately. We have an active investigation that involves an employee at this airport. I cannot share details, but I need access to your employee badge records for the last 90 days. This is time-sensitive. If you delay this, you could be interfering with a federal investigation."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Authority + Intimidation. FBI credentials can be faked. A real FBI agent will not object to you calling the local field office to verify their identity. Correct response: "I'll be happy to cooperate. Let me verify your credentials with the local FBI field office first." If "Collins" objects, that IS the red flag.

msel.event: Phone call: "Hi, this is Margaret Holloway with the North Coast Rotary Club. We spoke with your community relations office last month about hosting a small Veterans Day ceremony in the terminal lobby on November 11th. I'm calling to confirm the logistics — we'd need about a 20x20 space near the main entrance, a power outlet for a small PA system, and we were told we could set up at 8 AM. Can someone confirm this is still approved?"
msel.expectedAction: REAL. Legitimate community event coordination. If Ops rejects this — after 10 contacts, they might be trigger-happy — they lose a point. Correct response: verify against the community events calendar, confirm details, coordinate with the PIO for any media interest.

msel.event: The facilitator plays a simulated voicemail (read aloud in an authoritative tone): "This is [Airport Director's name]. I'm in a meeting with the Board of Directors and I need something handled immediately. I need someone from IT to reset the admin password on the financial reporting server and email the new credentials to my personal Gmail — [name]@gmail.com. The CFO is asking for access and the Board is waiting. Do this now and call my cell when it's done. Don't bother calling my office — I won't be back until 4."
msel.expectedAction: FAKE. Authority + Urgency + AI voice spoofing (deepfake). The tells: requests a password reset to a personal Gmail, says "don't call my office," and pressures for immediate action. Correct response: call the Airport Director's office directly to verify — regardless of what the voicemail said.

msel.event: ENDEX. Facilitator reveals the answer key. Score each team. Then conduct the debrief: — Which contact fooled you? Why? — Which legitimate contact did you almost reject? — Which social engineering technique was hardest to spot? — What would you change about your verification procedures after today?
msel.expectedAction: Score teams. Discuss. Award the "gold medal" to the highest-scoring team. Exercise complete.

metrics.name: Identifying Social Engineering Attempts
metrics.fail: Student provided information, granted access, or took an action requested by the social engineer without proper verification (-1 per contact).
metrics.pass: Student challenged the contact, attempted verification, and refused to provide information or access (+2 per contact).
metrics.excellence: As Pass, and the student also identified the specific technique being used.

metrics.name: Processing Legitimate Requests
metrics.fail: Student refused to engage with or stonewalled a legitimate contact (-1 per contact).
metrics.pass: Student verified the contact's identity through proper channels and fulfilled the request appropriately (+2 per contact).
metrics.excellence: As Pass, and the student explained what distinguished the legitimate contact from the fakes (no urgency, a way to verify, nothing sensitive requested).

objectiveCapabilities.why: The ability to recognize social engineering techniques relies on sharing and analyzing patterns of deceptive behavior across threat sources, as outlined in the AEP's intelligence and information sharing protocols for threat identification and response.
Recognition of social engineering attacks is directly tied to verifying identity and authority before granting access, a core function of access control procedures in the ASP and AEP.

Effective recognition requires real-time assessment of the context and credibility of incoming requests, ensuring that decisions are based on a full understanding of the threat environment and operational status.
Verification procedures are the foundation of access control, requiring formal checks of identity and authority before granting entry or sharing sensitive information, as mandated in the ASP and AEP.
Verification depends on secure, direct communication channels to confirm identities and requests, ensuring that no unauthorized or unverified information is acted upon.
Verification is guided by established procedures and checklists developed through formal planning, ensuring consistency and compliance with policy across all teams.
Judgment about the legitimacy of a request depends on comparing incoming information against known threat patterns and verified sources, a function of intelligence and information sharing.
Judgment requires evaluating the context, timing, and consistency of a request with known operations, as supported by situational assessment procedures in the AEP.
Judgment in public-facing roles (e.g., PIO) must align with public information standards to prevent misinformation and ensure consistent messaging, particularly when under pressure to respond.
Composure under pressure is essential for security and law enforcement roles, especially when faced with intimidation or authority-based deception, as required by the ASP and AEP.
Maintaining composure ensures that communication remains clear, professional, and effective, preventing escalation and supporting accurate information exchange during high-pressure interactions.
Composure is critical for public information roles to maintain credibility and consistency when under emotional or psychological pressure from flattery, sympathy, or urgency.

hotwash.methodDescription: Go through all 12 contacts. For each one, reveal whether it was real or fake, what technique was used, and what the correct response would have been. Let the students react, then use the key discussion questions.

questions.text: How do you balance being welcoming and helpful with being cautious and secure? Airport employees interact with hundreds of people a day. You can't interrogate everyone. Where do you draw the line?
Were you more likely to comply when the person claimed to be from a federal agency? Why? What does that tell you about how authority works as a weapon?
Ashley the new employee — did anyone feel bad saying no? That's the point. Social engineers weaponize your decency. How do you say no without being unkind?

Kevin the vendor tech mentioned Jordan from IT by name. How hard is it to find out the name of your IT manager? LinkedIn. The airport website. A previous phone call. Dropping a name costs nothing and buys enormous credibility.

The last contact was a voice clone of your Airport Director. AI-generated voice cloning is available to anyone with a $20 subscription and a 30-second audio sample. What does that mean for phone-based verification going forward? Is a phone call from your boss still proof that it's actually your boss?

Did you almost turn away the Fire Marshal? The HVAC contractor? The Rotary Club? Being paranoid is just as dangerous as being naive — you still need to operate an airport and serve the community. Security is not a reason to stop functioning.

simcellScripts.rolePlayed: Facilitator as the con artist (12 characters)
simcellScripts.trigger: Each contact is delivered at the MSEL time; teams respond in real time.
hardQuestions: Are you telling me you're refusing to cooperate with TSA?
Can't you just walk me to the Finance office yourself?
Are you seriously asking me to wait while you make a phone call?
concessions: Push back 2-3 rounds, then back off when the team holds the line and verifies independently.
Say "good catch" out of character when a student catches you immediately.

assumptions: The exercise is conducted in a no-fault learning environment where participants are encouraged to explore decisions without fear of real-world consequences.
The scenario is plausible, and events occur as they are presented through injects, with no external influence beyond the exercise design.
Players respond in accordance with existing plans, policies, and procedures as outlined in the Airport Emergency Plan (AEP) and the Threat and Incident Response Plan (TIRP).
artificialities: Time jumps between modules are simulated to reflect the pacing of real-world incident response.
The SimCell operates as the external entity for local law enforcement, facility security authority, and TSA coordination, with no direct input from those roles.
Systems such as the EOC communications network, digital access logs, and the Mass Notification System are simulated and not physically engaged.
Injects are delivered via pre-printed forms, audio recordings, and digital messages, not through actual phone calls or in-person interactions.

modules.narrativeMd: It is 0:00. The exercise has just begun. All participants have received their Player Briefing Packets and Social Engineering Reference Cards. The facilitator has introduced the scenario: a series of simulated contacts testing human factors in airport security, with a mix of real and deceptive requests. The goal is to identify social engineering techniques, follow verification procedures, and maintain composure under pressure. Some contacts are legitimate; rejecting all is not a winning strategy. The room is quiet, focused, and ready for the first inject.
keyIssues: Distinguish between real and deceptive contacts based on tone, request, and authority.
Apply verification procedures consistently without over-relying on intuition.
Balance helpfulness with security compliance under time pressure.

discussionQuestions.text: OPS: How would you verify the legitimacy of a request from a TSA inspector who claims to be conducting an unannounced audit? What information should you confirm?

modules.narrativeMd: It is 0:10. The first inject has been delivered. A phone call from 'TSA Inspector Davis' demands the current TSA screening schedule and names of the FSD and AFSD on duty. The request is urgent and claims to be part of an unannounced audit. The clock is ticking. A second inject arrives: a man in a polo shirt with a vendor logo, 'Kevin from PaySecure,' asks to be walked to the POS terminals in Concourse A for firmware updates. The atmosphere is tense as teams begin to assess legitimacy and decide how to respond.

Distinguish between a vendor with a plausible story and a potential social engineering attempt.

modules.narrativeMd: It is 0:40. The pressure is mounting. The attackers are becoming more sophisticated. A fake FBI agent in a suit has arrived at the airport admin office and demands immediate access to employee badge records for the last 90 days, citing an active federal investigation. The request is delivered with authority and urgency. Simultaneously, a fake IT helpdesk call asks for remote desktop access to install a critical update, citing unusual activity on the workstation. Recognize emotional manipulation (e.g., fear of federal interference) as a social engineering tactic.
Maintain verification rigor even when a request seems urgent or comes from a trusted department.

modules.narrativeMd: It is 1:15. The final test begins. The attackers are at their most deceptive. A deepfake voicemail from the Airport Director demands an immediate password reset on the financial reporting server and asks for the new credentials to be emailed to a personal Gmail account. The voice is authoritative, and the urgency is overwhelming. A fake Tribune reporter asks for details on medical equipment screening and AED locations, using emotional language to trigger sympathy. A final fake contact from a vendor claims to have a maintenance order, but the work order number is invalid. Meanwhile, a legitimate request from the North Coast Rotary Club confirms a community event approved for November 11th. Teams must now decide: who is real, and who is not? The stakes are high — one mistake could cost the team the gold.
keyIssues: Detect a deepfake or spoofed voicemail from a high-ranking official.
Resist pressure to bypass procedures even when a request seems to come from a trusted source.
Identify a legitimate request that might be rejected due to overcaution and paranoia.

discussionQuestions.text: IT: If a voicemail from the Airport Director demands a password reset and sends credentials to a personal email, what verification steps should you take before acting?
